title: Cranberry Juice for a Hangover: Does It Help or Flush Alcohol?
excerpt: Is cranberry juice good for a hangover? What it can and can't do, why it doesn't flush out alcohol or detox your liver, when its acidity backfires, and what to drink instead.
metaDescription: Does cranberry juice help a hangover? Why it won't flush out alcohol or detox your liver, when its acidity backfires, and better drinks to try instead.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** cranberry juice won't cure a hangover, and it doesn't detox your body or flush alcohol out faster. What it can do is give you some fluid and quick sugar on a morning when food feels hard to face. That's a real but small benefit, and plain water plus a bit of food does most of the same job. Cranberry juice's reputation mostly comes from two places: its genuine (if modest) role in preventing repeat urinary tract infections, and decades of being sold as a "cleansing" drink. Neither of those has much to do with a hangover.

**The quick rules:** If your stomach feels fine and you like it, a small glass of cranberry juice alongside water is a reasonable part of a hangover morning. If you have heartburn, a burning stomach, or you've been vomiting, skip it for now, because cranberry juice is one of the more acidic juices you can drink. Check whether you're drinking pure juice or "cranberry juice cocktail," since the cocktail is mostly added sugar. Don't use it to try to sober up, pass a test, or "cleanse" your liver. And if you take warfarin, check with your doctor before drinking much of it.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is unpleasant but fades within about a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe stomach pain, you're confused or very hard to wake, you have a seizure, or you're getting worse instead of better. If someone is passed out and can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin, call 911: that's alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and no juice will help. If you notice burning when you pee that lasts more than a day, or you have fever, pain in your back or side, or blood in your urine, see a doctor, because that may be an infection rather than a hangover.

## Why Cranberry Juice Became a "Hangover Drink"

Cranberry juice has a health halo that few other drinks can match. For generations it has been the drink people reach for when they want to "flush out" their system. It's in nearly every bar, because it's the base of the vodka cranberry (also called a Cape Codder) and the Cosmopolitan. And its tart, cold taste feels refreshing when you wake up dry-mouthed and tired.

Some of that reputation is earned. Cranberries contain plant compounds that have been studied for urinary tract health, and that research is real. But somewhere along the way, "good for your bladder" turned into "good for cleansing your body," and from there into "good for clearing out alcohol." That last step isn't supported by evidence.

To see where cranberry juice can and can't help, it's useful to know what actually causes a hangover. Researchers don't fully agree, but the main pieces seem to be:

- **Mild dehydration.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, sometimes called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more than you drink. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) explains this in detail.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, and people with worse hangovers tend to have higher levels of inflammatory signals in their blood.
- **Acetaldehyde.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that's normally cleared quickly but may contribute to how rough you feel.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep but breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which is why nausea and heartburn are common the morning after.
- **Low blood sugar.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar, especially if you drank without eating, which can add to shakiness, weakness, and fatigue.

Cranberry juice can nudge one or two of these slightly (fluid and blood sugar). It does nothing meaningful for the rest.

## What's Actually in a Glass of Cranberry Juice

The first thing to know is that "cranberry juice" on a store shelf can mean two very different products.

**Pure (100%) cranberry juice.** This is juice pressed from cranberries with nothing else added. It's intensely tart, and many people find it hard to drink straight. It contains natural sugars, a modest amount of vitamin C, and plant compounds called polyphenols, including a group called proanthocyanidins (PACs) that get most of the research attention.

**Cranberry juice cocktail.** This is what most people picture when they think of cranberry juice. It's a blend of cranberry juice, water, and added sugar (or another sweetener), and often only a minority of it is actual cranberry juice. Many brands also add vitamin C. It's sweeter and easier to drink, but nutritionally it's closer to a soft drink with some fruit in it.

**"Light" or diet versions.** These swap some or all of the sugar for low-calorie sweeteners. They taste closer to the cocktail with fewer calories, but they also give you less of the quick sugar that's the one thing juice actually offers a hangover.

**Blends.** Many "cranberry" drinks are really blends of apple, grape, and cranberry juice. Those are usually sweeter and less acidic than pure cranberry juice.

Here's a rough comparison of what matters for a hangover:

| Drink | Fluid | Quick sugar | Sodium (helps you hold fluid) | Acidity | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Water | Yes | None | None | Neutral | The baseline. Cheap and gentle. |
| Pure cranberry juice | Yes | Moderate | Very little | High | Very tart; can sting a sore stomach |
| Cranberry juice cocktail | Yes | High (mostly added) | Very little | High | Closer to a soft drink |
| Orange juice | Yes | Moderate | Very little | Moderate to high | More potassium than cranberry |
| Coconut water | Yes | Low to moderate | Low | Low | Gentle; good potassium |
| Electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution | Yes | Low to moderate | Yes | Low to moderate | Best after vomiting or sweating |

Values vary by brand, so read the label. The pattern is the useful part: cranberry juice brings fluid and sugar, but almost no sodium and a lot of acid.

## Does Cranberry Juice Help a Hangover? What the Evidence Says

As far as we can find, there are no good clinical trials testing cranberry juice as a hangover treatment in people. So any claim that it "works" for hangovers is borrowing from other research or from tradition. Here's what each of the common claims is actually based on.

### Claim 1: "It hydrates you"

True, in the same way any liquid does. Cranberry juice is mostly water, so a glass of it counts toward getting your fluids back. But it isn't better than water for this, and a very sugary drink isn't the most efficient way to rehydrate. When a drink has a lot of sugar and little salt, your body doesn't absorb the fluid any faster than plain water, and very sweet drinks can upset a queasy stomach. If you sweated a lot or vomited, a drink with sodium does a better job. Our guide on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) goes into what rehydration can and can't fix.

### Claim 2: "It gives you energy"

Partly true. The sugar in cranberry juice, especially the cocktail, gets into your blood quickly. If you drank on an empty stomach and your blood sugar is low, that can take the edge off shakiness and weakness. But a quick sugar hit wears off quickly too. Pairing juice with real food (toast, eggs, oatmeal, a banana) gives you steadier energy.

### Claim 3: "The antioxidants fight the damage"

This is the weakest claim. Cranberries are rich in polyphenols, which act as antioxidants in lab tests, and alcohol does cause oxidative stress (a kind of chemical wear and tear on cells). But "antioxidant in a test tube" rarely translates into "noticeable effect in a person the next morning." There is no good evidence that drinking cranberry juice reduces hangover symptoms through its antioxidants or anything else.

### Claim 4: "The vitamin C helps"

Many cranberry juice cocktails are fortified with vitamin C, so a glass can contain a fair amount. But vitamin C itself has weak evidence as a hangover remedy, and if you eat a normal diet you're probably not short of it. Our deeper look at [orange juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover) covers the vitamin C research, and the same conclusion applies here.

The honest summary is that cranberry juice is a pleasant way to get some fluid and calories. Nothing specific to cranberries has been shown to help a hangover.

## Does Cranberry Juice Flush Alcohol Out of Your System?

No. This is probably the most common belief about cranberry juice and alcohol, and it's simply not how the body works.

Once alcohol is in your bloodstream, your liver breaks most of it down at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults, though that varies with body size, sex, genetics, and drinking habits. Only a small fraction leaves unchanged through your breath, sweat, and urine. Drinking more fluid makes you pee more, but it doesn't make your liver work faster, so it doesn't lower your blood alcohol level any quicker.

That means cranberry juice, water, coffee, a cold shower, or a big meal the morning after will not sober you up. If you drank a lot late at night, you may still be over the legal driving limit in the morning no matter how much juice you've had. Our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) explains what does and doesn't change the clearance rate (spoiler: mostly time).

### What about passing an alcohol urine test?

Cranberry juice is sometimes passed around as a trick for clearing alcohol from your urine before a test. It doesn't work. Many alcohol urine tests look for by-products such as ethyl glucuronide (EtG), which can stay detectable for a day or more after drinking, longer after heavy drinking. Drinking large amounts of any fluid can dilute your urine, but testing labs routinely check for diluted samples and may treat them as suspicious or ask for a retest. Drinking huge amounts of fluid in a short time can also be dangerous, because it can drive your blood sodium too low. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your urine](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-urine) covers detection windows in more detail.

## The Cranberry Juice "Detox" Myth

You'll often see cranberry juice sold or recommended as a liver detox or a "cleanse" after a big weekend. There is no good evidence for this.

Your liver and kidneys are your detox system. They clear alcohol and its by-products around the clock without any special drink. No juice has been shown to make them do it faster or better in healthy people. Some lab and animal studies have looked at cranberry extracts and markers of liver health, and a few small human studies have explored cranberry in people with fatty liver disease, but that research is early and doesn't mean a bottle of cranberry juice cleans up after a night of drinking.

It's also worth knowing that the sweetened versions add a real dose of sugar. Your liver processes the fructose in sugary drinks, and regularly drinking a lot of sugar-sweetened beverages is linked to fatty liver disease, the same condition heavy drinking can cause. Drinking large amounts of cranberry juice cocktail as a "liver cleanse" is, if anything, a step in the wrong direction.

If you care about your liver after drinking, the things that actually matter are less exciting: drinking less, having alcohol-free days during the week, not drinking on an empty stomach, and being careful with acetaminophen (Tylenol) when you've been drinking heavily. Our article on [liver detox methods versus marketing myths](/never-hungover/best-liver-detox-science-based-methods-vs-marketing-myths-2025) goes through the claims one by one.

## The Acidity Problem: When Cranberry Juice Makes It Worse

Pure cranberry juice is one of the most acidic juices on the shelf, which is part of why it tastes so sharp. That matters on a hangover morning, because alcohol has already done a number on your stomach. It irritates the stomach lining, increases acid production, and relaxes the valve at the bottom of your esophagus that normally keeps acid where it belongs. That combination is why so many people wake up with heartburn, a burning stomach, or nausea after drinking.

Pouring a very acidic drink on top of that can make it sting more. You're most likely to notice it if:

- You have heartburn or reflux, either regularly or just after drinking.
- Your stomach feels raw, burning, or empty.
- You've been vomiting, which also irritates your throat and esophagus.
- You're drinking pure cranberry juice rather than a diluted or blended version.

If any of those apply, start with water, an electrolyte drink, or coconut water, plus something bland like toast or crackers, and come back to juice later once things settle. If you still want cranberry juice, dilute it with water or sparkling water, and have it with food rather than on an empty stomach. Our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) has more on calming a burning stomach.

### Can cranberry juice upset your stomach in other ways?

Yes. Large amounts of any fruit juice can loosen your stools, partly because of the sugar, and alcohol already speeds up your gut. If you're dealing with an upset stomach or loose stools the morning after, a big glass of sugary juice may not help. Smaller sips, more water, and plain food are gentler.

## Cranberry Juice, Alcohol, and Your Bladder

This is where cranberry juice's reputation comes from, so it's worth getting right.

### What the UTI research actually shows

Cranberries contain a type of proanthocyanidin that, in lab studies, makes it harder for certain bacteria to stick to the lining of the bladder. That's the theory behind using cranberry to prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs). A 2023 Cochrane review, which pools the results of many trials, concluded that cranberry products probably reduce the chance of repeat symptomatic UTIs in women who get them often, in children, and in some people after medical procedures. The evidence was less convincing for other groups, such as older adults in care homes.

Two important limits:

- **Prevention, not treatment.** Cranberry may lower the odds of getting another UTI. It doesn't treat an infection you already have. A UTI usually needs antibiotics, and leaving one untreated can let it spread to the kidneys.
- **It has nothing to do with alcohol.** None of this research suggests cranberry juice changes how your body handles alcohol or reduces a hangover.

### Burning when you pee after drinking

Many people notice their urine is darker or that it stings a bit after a night out. Often that's simply because you're mildly dehydrated, so your urine is more concentrated. Alcohol and caffeine can also irritate the bladder in some people, making you feel like you need to go more often or more urgently. Drinking water usually sorts this out within a day.

If the burning doesn't settle with fluids, or you have any of these, see a doctor rather than relying on cranberry juice:

- Burning or pain that lasts more than a day
- Needing to pee often but only passing small amounts
- Cloudy, strong-smelling, or bloody urine
- Fever, chills, or pain in your back or side (possible kidney infection)
- Symptoms during pregnancy

### Kidney stones

Cranberries contain oxalate, a compound that is part of the most common type of kidney stone. For most people, a normal glass of cranberry juice isn't a concern. But if you've had kidney stones before, especially calcium oxalate stones, it's worth asking your doctor whether you should limit cranberry products, and not drinking large amounts of it every day "for your kidneys." Staying well hydrated with water is one of the most consistent pieces of stone-prevention advice.

## Vodka Cranberry and Cosmopolitans: Not a Hangover Cure

Because cranberry juice is such a common mixer, some people assume a vodka cranberry is a "lighter" or "cleaner" drink that's less likely to cause a hangover. There's a grain of truth and a lot of wishful thinking in that.

The grain of truth: vodka is a clear, highly filtered spirit, and it contains fewer congeners (by-products of fermentation and aging) than dark drinks like bourbon, brandy, or red wine. Some research has found that drinks high in congeners can produce somewhat worse hangovers at the same blood alcohol level. So vodka may be a little kinder than whiskey, drink for drink.

The wishful thinking: the biggest factor in how bad your hangover is remains how much alcohol you drink. A vodka cranberry still contains a full shot of alcohol, and the juice adds sugar and masks the taste of the spirit, which makes the drink easy to finish fast and easy to order again. A night of five or six vodka cranberries will produce a hangover regardless of the mixer.

Adding more cranberry juice to the next morning's drink, or having a "hair of the dog" vodka cranberry, won't help either. More alcohol just postpones the hangover and adds to the total your liver has to clear.

If you do drink vodka cranberries, a few habits help:

- **Ask for a longer pour of juice or soda, not a double.** It slows you down.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks helps with both pace and fluid.
- **Eat beforehand.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Keep count.** Sweet mixed drinks are easy to lose track of.

## Cranberry Juice and Medications

For most people, a glass of cranberry juice is harmless. A few situations call for more care, especially when alcohol is also involved.

- **Warfarin (Coumadin).** There have been case reports of people on warfarin whose blood-clotting test results rose after drinking large amounts of cranberry juice, and at least one regulator issued caution about it years ago. Later controlled studies have been mixed, and many found little effect at moderate amounts. The practical advice from most clinicians is to avoid suddenly drinking a lot of cranberry juice, keep your intake modest and consistent, and tell your doctor if you change it. Alcohol also changes how warfarin works, so a heavy night followed by a big cranberry juice "cleanse" is a combination worth avoiding.
- **Diabetes medicines.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar, and sweetened cranberry juice raises it quickly. If you use insulin or medicines that lower blood sugar, check your levels rather than guessing, and don't use juice as your only fix for a low. Follow the plan your care team gave you.
- **Pain relievers the morning after.** Cranberry juice doesn't change how painkillers work, but alcohol does. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) adds strain to the liver in people who drink heavily, and ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate the stomach. Read the alcohol warnings on the label, take the lowest dose that works, and eat first.
- **Cranberry supplements.** Concentrated cranberry pills or extracts deliver more of the active compounds than juice. If you take any prescription medicine, ask a pharmacist before adding them.

When in doubt, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. They can look at your full medication list and give you advice that fits your situation.

## Cranberry Juice vs. Other Hangover Drinks

If you're standing in front of the fridge wondering what to reach for, here's how cranberry juice stacks up:

- **Versus water:** Water is gentler on the stomach, has no sugar, and hydrates just as well for most hangovers. Cranberry juice adds calories and taste, nothing more.
- **Versus orange juice:** Both are acidic and sugary. Orange juice has more potassium and natural vitamin C; cranberry juice cocktail is often fortified with vitamin C but has less potassium. Neither has an edge as a hangover remedy.
- **Versus coconut water:** Coconut water is lower in acid and naturally contains potassium, so it's usually easier on a sore stomach. Our guide to [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) covers its pros and cons.
- **Versus electrolyte drinks:** If you sweated a lot, vomited, or had diarrhea, a drink with sodium and potassium (like an oral rehydration solution) is the better choice. Our comparison of [electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) breaks down the main options.
- **Versus coffee:** Coffee may help a caffeine-withdrawal headache if you drink it daily, but it can also irritate the stomach. It doesn't rehydrate you well on its own.

For a wider view, our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) ranks the common choices by what they can realistically do.

## How to Use Cranberry Juice Sensibly the Morning After

If you enjoy cranberry juice and want it in your hangover routine, here's a simple way to use it where it helps and avoid it where it doesn't:

1. **Start with water.** A big glass when you wake up, then keep sipping. Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're catching up.
2. **Check your stomach.** If it's calm, a small glass (around 4 to 8 ounces) of cranberry juice is fine. If it's burning, queasy, or you've been sick, choose water, an electrolyte drink, or coconut water first.
3. **Pick the right bottle.** Pure cranberry juice diluted with water or sparkling water is less sugary than a cocktail. A cocktail gives more quick sugar if that's what you need, but don't drink a whole bottle.
4. **Eat something real.** Toast, eggs, oatmeal, or a banana give steadier energy and help buffer the acid and sugar.
5. **Add electrolytes if you lost fluid.** Sodium matters more than anything in cranberry juice if you sweated or vomited.
6. **Rest.** Time is the only thing that reliably ends a hangover.
7. **Don't drive until the alcohol has cleared.** Juice doesn't lower your blood alcohol level.

## Prevention Beats Any Morning Drink

No glass of juice can undo a heavy night. The habits that most reliably reduce hangovers happen before and during drinking: eating a proper meal first, pacing yourself, alternating alcoholic drinks with water, choosing lower-strength drinks, and simply drinking less. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the steps with the best support.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven, and it doesn't replace eating, hydrating, or drinking less. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check with your doctor before adding any supplement.

To see how cranberry compares with the other options, read our [best juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-juice-for-hangover) ranking and our guide to [apple juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/apple-juice-for-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Cranberry juice can help a mild hangover a little by giving you fluid and quick sugar, and nothing more specific than that.
- It doesn't flush alcohol out, sober you up, help you pass a urine test, or detox your liver. Only time clears alcohol.
- It's very acidic. If you have heartburn, a burning stomach, or you've been vomiting, start with water or an electrolyte drink instead.
- Cranberry juice cocktail is mostly added sugar. Pure juice diluted with water is a lighter option.
- Its real claim to fame is a modest role in preventing repeat UTIs, which doesn't extend to treating an infection or to hangovers.
- If you take warfarin, have had kidney stones, or manage diabetes, check with your doctor before drinking much of it.
- The things that actually help are water, food, rest, and drinking less next time.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is cranberry juice good for a hangover?**

It can help a little, mostly because it's fluid plus some easy sugar when solid food feels hard. There is no good evidence that cranberry juice, or anything special in cranberries, shortens a hangover or clears alcohol faster. Water, an electrolyte drink if you sweated or vomited, some food, and rest do most of the work. If you like cranberry juice, a small glass alongside water is fine.

**Does cranberry juice flush alcohol out of your system?**

No. Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults, and no juice speeds that up in a way you'd notice. Cranberry juice may make you pee more simply because you're drinking more liquid, but that doesn't remove alcohol faster or lower your blood alcohol level. Only time sobers you up.

**Does cranberry juice detox your liver after drinking?**

No. Your liver and kidneys clear alcohol and its by-products on their own, and there is no good evidence that cranberry juice speeds that up or 'cleanses' the liver. Cranberries do contain antioxidant plant compounds, but studies on liver health are small and early. The most useful thing for your liver is drinking less and giving it alcohol-free days.

**Can cranberry juice help you pass an alcohol urine test?**

No. Alcohol urine tests usually look for by-products such as ethyl glucuronide (EtG), which can show up for a day or more after drinking. Drinking lots of cranberry juice or water may dilute your urine, but labs check for diluted samples and may flag or reject them. It does not remove the markers from your body.

**Is pure cranberry juice better than cranberry juice cocktail for a hangover?**

Neither is a hangover remedy, but they're different drinks. Pure, unsweetened cranberry juice is very tart and acidic, with natural sugar but nothing added. Cranberry juice cocktail is mostly water and added sugar with a smaller share of juice. If your stomach is fine and you want quick calories, either works in a small glass. If your stomach is sore, pure cranberry juice is likely to sting more, so dilute it or choose water or an electrolyte drink.

**Does cranberry juice help with burning when you pee after drinking?**

Usually not much. Burning after a night out is often from concentrated urine because you're a bit dehydrated, and water is the fix. Cranberry products have some evidence for lowering the chance of repeat urinary tract infections in people who get them often, but they don't treat an infection that's already started. If burning lasts more than a day, or you have fever, back or side pain, or blood in your urine, see a doctor.

**Can I drink cranberry juice if I take warfarin?**

Ask your doctor or pharmacist first. There have been case reports of people on warfarin whose blood-clotting test results changed after drinking a lot of cranberry juice, and studies since then have been mixed. Many clinicians advise people on warfarin to keep cranberry intake small and steady rather than suddenly drinking large amounts. Alcohol also affects warfarin, so heavy drinking and a big cranberry juice binge the morning after is a combination worth avoiding.

**Is a vodka cranberry less likely to cause a hangover?**

Not really. Vodka is a clear spirit and is lower in congeners (by-products of fermentation that may worsen hangovers) than dark liquors like bourbon, so it may be slightly kinder than some drinks. But the main driver of a hangover is how much alcohol you drink. The cranberry juice adds sugar and makes the drink easy to finish quickly, which can make it easier to overdo it.
